subject: Habitat overlap, recursion visit and time spent in  habitat patches!

messages.author: 51869baac44f285f
messages.subject: Habitat overlap, recursion visit and time spent in  habitat patches!
parts:
Hi Chris,
I am trying to identify the habitat patches that are frequently used along with the duration of time spent in those patches. Also, I want to estimate the habitat overlapped by individuals. The ctmm package must have these features, but I am not sure which one should I go with. I look forward for your advise.
Thank you!
Damber

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Habitat overlap, recursion visit and time spent in  habitat patches!
parts:
Hi Damber,

For the point estimate on fraction of time spent in a patch, you can take the occurrence distribution and export its PMF and sum the probability mass in the patches.

For a point estimate + confidence intervals, you need to resort to simulations. We plan to have tools for this in ctmm within ~1 year, kind of similar to the tools for estimating speed/distance.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Habitat overlap, recursion visit and time spent in habitat patches!
parts:
Hi Chris,
Thank you so much! This really worked for estimating time spent in highly used habitat patches. I also estimated home range overlap using overlap function, but again I am interested to quantify how many times (and when) do the individuals come in proximity to each other. This is very important aspect for my study because my target animal has territorial nature. So, I would appreciate your advise on this.
Thanks again for your help!
Best regards,
Damber

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Habitat overlap, recursion visit and time spent in habitat patches!
parts:
Hi Damber,

To estimate how often individuals encounter each other is something that will eventually be directly calculable in a rigorous way. We actually have some encounter related functionality coming very soon. But for the time being, that would require running simulations to calculate in a more sophisticated way than just running through the times and testing pairwise distance like you would without ctmm.

Best,
Chris
